query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) will exhibit superior resistance to tribo-corrosion degradation in high‐temperature molten salt environments compared to conventional duplex stainless steels because its dual‐phase microstructure promotes the formation of a noble‐element enriched protective surface layer.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA with a fine lamellar microstructure comprising an FCC protective phase (or FCC-derived phase) and a BCC/B2 phase.
generation.intervention: Expose the EHEA to a high-temperature molten salt environment under tribological (friction/wear) conditions.
generation.conditions: Testing in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt at temperatures such as 450 °C and 650 °C under cyclic mechanical loading that simulates frictional wear in addition to corrosive exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The dual-phase microstructure facilitates micro-galvanic coupling; the FCC (or L1_2/B2) phase acts as a barrier that, upon selective dissolution of the less noble BCC/B2 phase, leads to enrichment of noble elements at the surface.
generation.mechanism: Selective dissolution driven by micro-galvanic interactions between phases under high-temperature and mechanical stress conditions leads to the formation of a protective, oxidation-resistant surface layer enriched with noble elements. This enhanced surface layer mitigates further corrosion and reduces wear damage by increasing the local work function.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional duplex stainless steel (e.g., DS2205), the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA will show significantly lower corrosion rates and reduced wear (tribo-corrosion), with improvements potentially on the order of several-fold reduction in degradation rates under similar test conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance of traditional structural alloys such as duplex stainless steel 2205 when exposed to similar high-temperature molten salt environments with tribological stresses.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvement is expected primarily within the studied temperature range (approximately 450 °C to 650 °C) in molten salt conditions; its efficacy under other environmental conditions or significantly different wear regimes remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvement levels under combined tribological and corrosive stresses are uncertain and require further experimental validation. Additionally, the durability of the protective layer under prolonged dynamic mechanical wear is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and a baseline duplex stainless steel (DS2205). Prepare test specimens and subject them to a high-temperature molten salt environment (using a NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 eutectic mixture) at controlled temperatures (450 °C and 650 °C) while simultaneously applying cyclic tribological loading using a reciprocating tribometer. Test duration should be sufficient to capture both initial corrosion and wear behavior.
measurements: Wear scar depth and morphology via microscopy
Surface composition analysis (e.g., XPS or EDS) to detect noble-element enrichment
Electrochemical potential mapping (e.g., SKP) to assess passive layer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in combined corrosion and wear rates compared to the DS2205 baseline—specifically, if no protective phase formation or noble-element surface enrichment is observed—the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. The world economy is highly dependent on fossil fuels to meet persistent energy demands, which results in carbon emissions and negative environmental impacts. This is driving the global search for sustainable and alternative energy sources [ [1] ], solar energy being one of the most viable and clean options [ [2] ]. The global capacity for concentrating solar power (CSP) systems has increased fifteen-fold over the last two decades [ [3] ]. The solar power conversion systems in CSP operate with advanced fluids above 400 °C [ [4] ], using molten salts such as solar salt [ [5] ], Hitec salt [ [6] ], and MgNaK chlorides [ [7] ]. In particular, the ternary MgNaK chloride (MgCl 2 -NaCl-KCl) eutectic salt mixture has high thermal stability and is more cost effective compared to other molten salts [ [8] , [9] ]. This allows CSP to operate at higher temperatures for higher efficiency of thermal-to-electrical energy conversion and reduces the cost of electricity. However, degradation of structural materials in a molten salt environment remains a critical concern in CSP systems [ [9] , [10] ].
